title: Sea Watch Off by No More Than 10 Nautical Miles: Why Was the £20,000 Prize Split in Two?
description:
Over 300 years ago, Britain offered £20,000 for a way for ships at sea to find their longitude. In 1765, Parliament wrote the sea trial of John Harrison's marine watch into an Act: from Portsmouth to Bridgetown, Barbados, the ship fixed its longitude by this watch and was never off by more than ten geographical miles (roughly nautical miles), against a top-prize limit of thirty. But the same Act split the prize in two: the first half required him to make the watch's construction public within six months and to sign over his first three machines and this watch to the Board of Longitude; the second half required watches like it to be made and then tested within the same limit.

This episode follows the records in order: the three-tier prize of 1714; "one degree apart, noon differs by about four minutes"; his son William waiting five months at Portsmouth; the Jamaica voyage, which earned only a finding of "considerable use" and a £2,500 advance; the watch taken apart on August 22, 1765, before the men the Board sent; the land test at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, from May 1766; Harrison's pamphlet of rebuttal, printed in 1767; and the 1773 Act of Parliament that recorded "48 years" and authorized "a further reward" of up to £8,750.

Limits: the ten geographical miles is the finding the 1765 Act adopted; this episode does not recompute the ship's logs. Harrison's criticisms of the Board and of Maskelyne are his own account, not an independent ruling. The 1773 further reward is not the second half of the original £20,000, and the Act does not list how much of each half was actually paid. Sources are fixed OCR versions of the 1765 and 1773 Acts of the British Parliament and Harrison's 1767 pamphlet, listed in the references below.

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; the watch's interior and the documents are illustrative.

Data as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

chapters.prize-1714: 1714: a prize for longitude at sea

lg101.text: Your phone map shows where you are in one second.

lg102.text: Over 300 years ago, ships couldn't tell how far east or west they'd gone, so Britain offered £20,000.

lg103.text: In 1765, Parliament wrote a marine watch's sea trial into an Act.

lg104.text: Top prize: error within 30 geographical miles. The Act says this watch stayed within it.

lg105.text: Surely, then, the whole sum should go to Harrison, the watchmaker?

lg106.text: But that same Act split the prize into two halves.

lg107.text: Stranger still, the next year: the watch went to an observatory, and an astronomer logged daily whether it ran fast or slow.

lg108.text: This file follows two Acts and Harrison's own pamphlet, from the prize to the last payment.

lg109.text: Why couldn't a watch that passed its sea trial get the whole prize?

lg201.text: That prize from the start was set by an Act of 1714.

lg202.text: Sailing west, there's only sea all around, and no signpost marked with longitude.

lg203.text: You may ask: why not just look up at the sun?

lg204.text: The sun crosses overhead every day, but noon isn't at the same moment everywhere.

lg205.text: Earth turns once in 24 hours, and maps divide that turn into 360 degrees.

lg206.text: Harrison put it simply: one degree apart, noon differs by about four minutes.

lg207.text: So a ship just needs a watch keeping the home port's time all the way.

lg208.text: The watch says it's already noon at port, but the sun isn't overhead yet; what does the gap mean?

lg209.text: How far west the ship has gone: the longer the gap, the farther.

lg210.text: Simple, right? When I first read this, I thought it was long solved.

lg211.text: The trouble is, ships roll and weather changes; would a clock that runs fine on shore hold up at sea?

lg212.text: That Act let any method at all be tried at sea, with the prize in three tiers.

lg214.text: The top tier was that 30 from the start, paired with the £20,000.

lg215.text: Geographical mile: about a nautical mile today.

lg216.text: A good watch alone did not earn it: it had to be tried at sea, judged by the Board of Longitude.

lg217.text: So what kind of clock would Harrison take on board?

lg301.text: He'd made three timekeepers; the fourth was different: a watch you could carry.

lg302.text: It wasn't a wall pendulum clock on a ship; it was made to handle that rolling.

lg303.text: He still had the first three; in a few years, Parliament would demand them.

lg304.text: For this watch, he dealt with the Board for years, and finally won an official sea trial.

lg306.text: Not him, but his son, William.

lg307.text: William was sent to Portsmouth first, awaiting official orders for five months.

lg308.text: Imagine idling at port with your father's years of work,

lg309.text: wouldn't you doubt the voyage would happen?

lg310.text: At last the ship sailed. William took the watch aboard the Royal Navy's HMS Deptford, bound for Jamaica.

lg311.text: Reading this, I worried for him.

lg312.text: Would a precise first trip win him the top tier outright?

lg401.text: Not so fast. Coming home, William switched to the Merlin, with the watch.

lg402.text: Next, astronomical readings at both places were checked against the watch; would the results match?

lg403.text: The Board had a method, Harrison had both places' observations, and they disagreed.

lg404.text: Like you and a friend checking the same receipts and getting different totals.

lg405.text: He wanted a checker he trusted; did the Board agree?

lg407.text: He also said it was years before he saw the Board's calculations.

lg408.text: Keep in mind, all of this is Harrison's account alone; who got it wrong, I won't judge for him.

lg409.text: So how did the law record this voyage?

lg410.text: The Act's finding was narrow: most of the Board held that the watch was of considerable use.

lg411.text: So he got £2,500 first, written as counting toward any prize he might later receive.

lg412.text: That was only an eighth of the top prize; the top tier had not yet been awarded to him.

lg413.text: The first trip left many disputes; could another West Indies run settle them?

lg501.text: Harrison sought another trial; William sailed again with the same watch.

lg502.text: This time from Portsmouth, across the Atlantic, to Bridgetown, Barbados.

lg503.text: The result is the line from the start, written into the Act: it stayed within the limit.

lg504.text: How far off? The Act says the ship, fixing longitude by this watch, never erred beyond ten geographical miles.

lg505.text: At most a third of the limit: the finding Parliament adopted, not our own math.

lg506.text: Honestly, if the story stopped here, it'd be a happy ending.

lg507.text: By the 1714 rules, you'd probably say: isn't that the top tier?

lg508.text: But the same Act says it was doubtful how, under the old law, this money should be paid.

lg509.text: The Act's reason: only if fully explained, and if watches like it can be made, could it come into wide use.

lg510.text: I find the reason easy to grasp: Britain's ships can't all take turns with one watch.

lg511.text: Harrison disagreed: he felt the sea trial had already answered the key question.

lg512.text: You may ask: did Parliament look down on a clockmaker?

lg513.text: The same Act also rewarded tables of the Moon's position; that year, clocks and astronomy weren't a race only one could win.

lg514.text: What anyone felt isn't recorded, and I won't guess.

lg515.text: So the question lands here: one watch worked, but copying it, could you make others?

lg516.text: So what did each half from the start require?

lg601.text: First half: explain how it was built, and in only six months.

lg602.text: Six months to explain years of work so others could understand it.

lg603.text: And sign over the first three machines, plus this watch, to the Board for public use.

lg604.text: In other words, four things he spent all those years making were no longer his.

lg606.text: It came off the first half. And the second?

lg607.text: Harder still: watches like it had to be made, tested within half a degree, the same top limit.

lg608.text: And the Board had to be satisfied; how many, how tested, the Act didn't spell out.

lg609.text: If you were Harrison, back from two voyages to find a new rule added, how would you feel?

lg610.text: As Harrison put it: the voyages were done, yet the prize rules had changed.

lg611.text: But he complied: on August 22, 1765, he took the watch apart.

lg612.text: Before the men the Board sent, he explained it piece by piece.

lg613.text: I can hardly imagine how that felt: years of work taken apart in front of others.

lg614.text: By Harrison's account, on handover day, William brought the watch.

lg615.text: He says he received the first half of the prize.

lg616.text: But once handed over, who had charge of the watch?

lg701.text: Harrison says it went first to the Admiralty, then to the Royal Observatory, Greenwich.

lg702.text: That astronomer from the start was the Astronomer Royal, Maskelyne, who took it over in May 1766.

lg703.text: This was a test on land, completely unlike the two at sea.

lg704.text: In the end, Maskelyne questioned the watch's daily rate.

lg706.text: The next year, he printed his own pamphlet rebutting the test and its math.

lg707.text: His point: a watch needn't be exact to the second; if its rate is steady and known, you subtract it.

lg708.text: Like your clock that's always two minutes fast: handy, since you just subtract two.

lg709.text: The question is: can an adjusted watch be judged by a rate measured before?

lg710.text: Harrison says he reset its rate on purpose before handover, so the sea-trial rate can't judge it.

lg711.text: This is his own rebuttal; the pamphlet alone can't prove Maskelyne's test wrong.

lg712.text: Sadly, we lack Maskelyne's full report.

lg713.text: He also asked the Board to lend it back so other makers could copy it; he says they refused.

lg714.text: Awkward: the second half needed watches like it.

lg715.text: So how did it all end?

lg801.text: It ended in another Act: in 1773, Parliament wrote Harrison's name in again.

lg802.text: The Act says he worked on timekeeping at sea, unremittingly, for 48 years.

lg803.text: Reading that number, I paused a long while.

lg804.text: It also says he'd published its principles.

lg805.text: Remember the question? One watch worked, but copying it, could you make others?

lg806.text: The Act's answer: watches like it had been made, and were quite accurate.

lg807.text: But it doesn't say who made them, or list how far off each was at sea.

lg808.text: Believing it would help shipping and trade, Parliament authorized a new reward.

lg809.text: Up to £8,750, paid by the Treasurer of the Navy.

lg810.text: Like me, you may first think: is this the second half of the original prize?

lg811.text: The text says "a further reward", on top of money he'd already received.

lg812.text: Think of it as Parliament opening a new tab, not settling the old one.

lg813.text: Each original half's actual payout isn't listed; we won't infer it from the new sum.

lg814.text: Okay, back to the start: the watch answered if it was accurate at sea; Parliament wanted another: could watches like it be made?

lg815.text: If you were the judge, would you go by one sea trial, or wait for more watches like it? Tell me below.

lg816.text: This channel sticks to the record; subscribe to open the files with me.
